triage.name: Refractive Errors
triage.reason: Blurred vision complaint with a straightforward diagnosis by history and vision testing; limited but real clinical reasoning.

demographics: Myopia and astigmatism often begin in school-age children and progress through the teenage years
Presbyopia affects nearly everyone, typically starting around age 45
Refractive error is the most common type of vision problem worldwide

risk_factors.text: Family history of glasses or contact lenses

family_history: Parent or sibling who wears glasses or contact lenses
social_history: Prolonged near work (reading, screens) is often reported but is not a proven cause

chief_complaints.text: I have to squint to see the board or read signs
My eyes feel tired and I get headaches after reading or using the computer
I have to hold things farther away to read them

hpi.onset: Gradual; myopia and astigmatism often noticed in childhood or the teen years, presbyopia noticed in the mid-40s
hpi.duration: Weeks to years of slowly changing vision; presbyopia symptoms progress over years
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive blurring that worsens with distance (myopia) or with near work (hyperopia, presbyopia); often noticed first when vision is compared with a friend's or when a school or driving vision test is failed
hpi.location: Both eyes, usually symmetric though one eye may be worse
hpi.quality: Blurred, hazy or distorted vision; objects may look smeared or doubled at the edges
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; vision is usually still functional with squinting or moving closer
hpi.timing: Constant, but most noticeable with specific tasks such as driving at night, reading, or looking at a screen
relieving: Moving closer to or farther from the object

associated_symptoms.text: Headaches, often frontal or around the eyes, after visual tasks
Glare or halos around bright lights
Difficulty focusing when reading or using a computer

pertinent_negatives: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye
Flashes of light or new floaters
Curtain or shadow over part of the vision

positives.text: Eye strain with reading or screens

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children rarely complain of blur; they may sit very close to the TV, hold books close, squint, rub their eyes, or be noted to have trouble at school or on vision screening.
Presbyopia is nearly universal, and symptoms may be attributed to cataract or macular disease; glare and difficulty with night driving are more prominent.

atypical.how_it_differs: Fluctuating blood sugar can cause temporary refractive shifts, so blur may come and go and a new prescription may not be stable until glucose is controlled.

decision_points: If acuity improves with pinhole or refraction, the cause is refractive; if it does not, pursue retinal, optic nerve, or neurologic evaluation
Check acuity one eye at a time; a unilateral deficit changes the differential toward amblyopia, cataract, or retinal disease
In children, use cycloplegic refraction to uncover latent hyperopia and prevent amblyopia
New or changing blur in a patient with diabetes may reflect fluctuating glucose rather than a true change in refractive error; wait until glucose is stable before finalizing a prescription

differential.name: Cataract
differential.why_considered: Gradual painless blurring of vision in an older adult, often with glare and difficulty with night driving
differential.trigger: Blur that does not fully correct with refraction, or a lens opacity seen on slit-lamp examination

history: Progressive blur over months to years, often worse in bright light or at night
exam: Reduced visual acuity that may not fully improve with pinhole or refraction
Lens opacity or nuclear sclerosis on slit-lamp examination
Reduced red reflex
imaging: Ocular ultrasound showing lens opacity when the view is poor

differential.name: Diabetic retinopathy
differential.why_considered: Blurred vision in a patient with diabetes, which can fluctuate with glucose control and mimic a refractive change
differential.trigger: Diabetes with blurred vision, especially if acuity does not fully correct with refraction

history: Blur that fluctuates with blood sugar control
exam: Reduced acuity that may not fully correct with pinhole
Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, or neovascularization on dilated fundoscopy
labs: Elevated hemoglobin A1c or fluctuating glucose
imaging: Optical coherence tomography showing macular edema
Fluorescein angiography showing leakage or ischemia

differential.name: Glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Blurred vision and halos around lights, especially in older adults
differential.trigger: Halos, eye pain, or visual field loss with reduced acuity that does not correct with refraction

history: Gradual peripheral vision loss (open-angle) or sudden painful vision loss with nausea (angle-closure)
exam: Elevated intraocular pressure
Cupping of the optic disc
Reduced visual fields
Mid-dilated fixed pupil and corneal edema in acute angle-closure
imaging: Optical coherence tomography showing retinal nerve fiber layer thinning

differential.name: Age-related macular degeneration
differential.why_considered: Central blurring and distortion in older adults

history: Central blur or distortion rather than uniform blur
exam: Reduced central acuity with relatively preserved peripheral vision
Drusen, pigmentary changes, or subretinal fluid on fundoscopy
imaging: Optical coherence tomography showing drusen or subretinal fluid

differential.name: Amblyopia
differential.why_considered: Reduced vision in one eye in a child that may be mistaken for a refractive error

history: Often asymptomatic; detected on vision screening
May have a history of strabismus or anisometropia
exam: Reduced acuity in one eye that does not fully correct with refraction
Strabismus or anisometropia
Normal ocular structures

differential.name: Keratoconus
differential.why_considered: Progressive blurring and irregular astigmatism, often in adolescents or young adults

history: Progressive blur and frequent prescription changes
exam: Irregular astigmatism
Scissoring of the retinoscopic reflex
Munson sign or conical cornea in advanced cases
imaging: Corneal topography showing inferior steepening and irregular astigmatism

differential.name: Retinal detachment
differential.why_considered: Sudden onset of floaters, flashes, and a curtain-like visual loss that can be confused with refractive blur
differential.trigger: Sudden flashes, floaters, or a curtain over the vision

history: Sudden onset of flashes and floaters
Curtain or shadow over part of the visual field
May follow trauma or eye surgery
exam: Reduced visual field or acuity
Retinal tear or detachment on dilated fundoscopy
imaging: Ocular ultrasound showing retinal detachment when the view is obscured

differential.name: Optic neuritis
differential.why_considered: Subacute unilateral vision loss with pain on eye movement, often in young adults
differential.trigger: Pain with eye movement and reduced color vision

history: Unilateral vision loss over hours to days
exam: Afferent pupillary defect
Reduced color vision on Ishihara testing
Swollen or normal optic disc
labs: May have elevated inflammatory markers if associated with systemic disease
imaging: MRI showing enhancement of the optic nerve

severity.mild: Blurred vision only with specific tasks (driving at night, reading small print); acuity corrects to normal with lenses; no functional limitation
severity.moderate: Blurred vision interferes with daily activities such as reading, schoolwork, or driving; headaches and eye strain with prolonged visual tasks; corrects with lenses
severity.severe: Marked blurring that limits activities even with effort; high refractive error or anisometropia; may be associated with amblyopia in children or difficulty functioning without correction
severity.critical: Not applicable to uncomplicated refractive error; sudden severe vision loss or painful red eye suggests another diagnosis

red_flags.finding: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye
red_flags.meaning: Suggests retinal artery occlusion, retinal detachment, or vitreous hemorrhage; needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation
Suggests keratitis, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma; not a simple refractive error

red_flags.finding: Flashes of light or new floaters
red_flags.meaning: Suggests retinal tear or detachment; needs urgent dilated fundoscopic examination

red_flags.finding: Curtain or shadow over part of the vision
red_flags.meaning: Suggests retinal detachment; urgent ophthalmology referral

red_flags.finding: Reduced acuity that does not improve with pinhole or refraction
red_flags.meaning: Suggests retinal, optic nerve, or other non-refractive cause; needs further evaluation

red_flags.finding: Diplopia that persists with one eye covered
red_flags.meaning: Suggests neurologic or orbital cause rather than refractive error

complications.name: Amblyopia
clues: Child with uncorrected anisometropia or high refractive error
Reduced acuity in one eye that does not fully correct with lenses

complications.name: Strabismus
clues: Child with uncorrected hyperopia or anisometropia

complications.name: Reduced quality of life and safety risks
clues: Falls or accidents related to poor vision

complications.name: Progression to high myopia with retinal complications
clues: New flashes, floaters, or visual field loss

special_populations.differences: Young children rarely complain of blur; they may sit close to the TV, squint, or rub their eyes. Uncorrected refractive error can cause amblyopia and strabismus, so early detection and correction are critical. Cycloplegic refraction is often needed.

Presbyopia is nearly universal, and symptoms may be attributed to cataract or macular disease. Glare and difficulty with night driving are more prominent. Refractive changes may also be the first sign of cataract or diabetes.

Fluctuating blood sugar can cause temporary refractive shifts, so blur may come and go and a new prescription may not be stable until glucose is controlled. Diabetic retinopathy can also cause blurred vision.
Hormonal changes can cause temporary changes in corneal thickness and refractive error; vision may fluctuate. Pre-eclampsia can cause blurred vision and should be ruled out if sudden.

key_questions.question: What exactly is blurry — things far away, things up close, or both?
key_questions.looking_for: Distance blur suggests myopia; near blur suggests hyperopia or presbyopia; blur at all distances suggests astigmatism

key_questions.question: When did you first notice this, and has it changed since?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to years; sudden onset points to a non-refractive cause

key_questions.question: Does squinting, moving closer, or holding things farther away help?
key_questions.looking_for: Squinting or changing the viewing distance improves vision, which supports a refractive cause

key_questions.question: Do you wear glasses or contact lenses, and when was your last prescription?
key_questions.looking_for: Existing correction that is outdated or no longer working; recent prescription change

key_questions.question: Do you get headaches, eye strain, or tired eyes after reading or using a screen?
key_questions.looking_for: Asthenopia with near work, typical of hyperopia or presbyopia

key_questions.question: Is the blur worse in dim light or when driving at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Glare, halos, and night vision difficulty, which also raise concern for cataract

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family wear glasses or contact lenses?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of refractive error, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you had any eye pain, redness, discharge, or recent eye injury or surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain, redness, or trauma suggests infection, inflammation, or injury rather than simple refractive error

key_questions.question: Have you noticed sudden flashes of light, new floaters, or a curtain or shadow over part of your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of retinal tear or detachment, which require urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Is the blur in one eye or both eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral blur shifts the differential toward amblyopia, cataract, or retinal or optic nerve disease

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, and if so, how well controlled is your blood sugar?
key_questions.looking_for: Fluctuating glucose can cause temporary refractive shifts; diabetic retinopathy can also blur vision

key_questions.question: Do you take any medications that can affect vision, such as steroids or anticholinergics?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that can cause blurred vision or precipitate angle-closure glaucoma

reasoning_points: Gradual, painless, bilateral blurring of vision that is worse for specific viewing distances
Blur improves with squinting, pinhole testing, or the correct spectacle or contact lens correction
Eye strain, headaches, and squinting with prolonged visual tasks
Normal eye examination apart from reduced acuity: no pain, redness, discharge, or afferent pupillary defect
Normal fundoscopic examination and full visual fields, ruling out retinal or optic nerve disease
Refraction confirms the diagnosis when acuity corrects to normal or near-normal with lenses
Red flags such as sudden vision loss, flashes, floaters, or a curtain over the vision are absent

Young adult with clear distance blur that corrects with a pinhole and with glasses
Healthy 48-year-old who must hold reading material at arm's length
Normal eye examination apart from reduced acuity
medium: Patient with astigmatism and blur at all distances plus glare and night vision difficulty
Young adult with latent hyperopia unmasked only on cycloplegic refraction
Patient with diabetes whose blur fluctuates with glucose control
Adult with an outdated prescription and eye strain from prolonged screen use
hard: Child with unilateral reduced acuity from anisometropic amblyopia rather than simple refractive error
Older adult whose blur does not fully correct with refraction because of an underlying cataract
Patient with reduced acuity that persists through a pinhole, pointing to retinal or optic nerve disease
Patient with irregular astigmatism and poor best-corrected acuity suggesting keratoconus
